reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: Episodes of dystonia or choreoathetosis brought on by sustained or prolonged physical exertion, typically affecting the exercised limbs
Attacks come on after minutes of continuous exercise rather than at the sudden onset of movement, distinguishing it from the kinesigenic form
An important cause is glucose transporter type 1 (GLUT1) deficiency due to SLC2A1 mutations, which is treatable with a ketogenic diet
GLUT1-related cases may also have epilepsy, developmental problems and a low cerebrospinal fluid glucose relative to blood
The paroxysmal dyskinesia spectrum overlaps genetically with PRRT2-related disorders
Recognising a GLUT1 cause is critical because dietary therapy can dramatically improve symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia is a paroxysmal movement disorder in which prolonged exertion triggers transient involuntary movements without loss of consciousness. A major mechanism is impaired glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier from GLUT1 deficiency, so that sustained metabolic demand during exercise outstrips brain glucose supply and precipitates dyskinesia. Other cases relate to channel and synaptic-protein abnormalities within the broader paroxysmal dyskinesia and PRRT2 spectrum, reflecting episodic dysfunction of basal ganglia motor control.
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for SLC2A1 (GLUT1) and PRRT2
Paired cerebrospinal fluid and blood glucose to assess for GLUT1 deficiency
Detailed characterisation of triggers and episode semiology
MRI of the brain to exclude structural causes
Trial of ketogenic diet where GLUT1 deficiency is confirmed
redFlags: Associated seizures or developmental delay suggesting GLUT1 deficiency
Onset with atypical features suggesting a structural lesion
Frequent disabling attacks affecting daily function
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good, especially when a treatable cause such as GLUT1 deficiency is identified and managed with diet; many other cases are controllable and non-progressive.
pitfalls: Failing to test for GLUT1 deficiency and missing a diet-responsive cause
Confusing it with the kinesigenic form triggered by sudden movement
Mislabelling episodes as functional without genetic and metabolic workup
Overlooking coexisting epilepsy in GLUT1-related disease
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Institute a ketogenic or modified Atkins diet as the definitive treatment where GLUT1 deficiency is confirmed, providing ketone fuel to the glucose-starved brain
Advise pacing of exertion and pre-exercise carbohydrate intake to reduce attack frequency
Treat coexisting epilepsy, which is common in GLUT1 deficiency and also responds to the ketogenic diet
Confirm the diagnosis with SLC2A1 and PRRT2 genetic testing and paired cerebrospinal fluid-to-blood glucose, since recognising GLUT1 deficiency is critical
Involve a dietitian to supervise and monitor the ketogenic diet
Offer genetic counselling and coordinate movement-disorder neurology follow-up
